P.label: PSU categories
P.title: What a public sector undertaking is, and its three forms
P.law: Public sector undertakings are owned or controlled by the Central Government, any State Government or Governments, or partly by the Central Government and one or more State Governments. They are organised in three forms: (1) departmentally managed undertakings that are part and parcel of government activities; (2) government companies and deemed government companies set up under the Companies Act, 2013; (3) corporations set up under specific Acts of the legislature.
notes: Departmental undertakings: Indian Railways, Postal Services, Security Printing Press, Canteen Stores Department.
Statutory corporations: Life Insurance Corporation, Unit Trust of India.

Role: key role in socio-economic development: basic inputs (coal, oil, steel, minerals, cement, chemicals, fertilizers, heavy equipment) and public utilities (railways, postal and telecom, electricity, road transport). The private sector is now also allowed in electricity generation, telecom, etc.

Government company (s.2(45) Companies Act, 2013): not less than 51% of paid-up share capital held by the Central Government, any State Government(s), or partly by both; includes a subsidiary of such a company. See Audit of government companies.

P.label: Art. 148–151
P.title: C&AG — constitutional status (Articles 148–151) and the DPC Act, 1971
P.law: Government audit in India is performed by an independent constitutional authority, the Comptroller and Auditor General of India (C&AG), through the Indian Audit and Accounts Department. The Constitution gives the C&AG a special status and safeguards his independence.
notes: Art. 148: appointed by the President; removal only by a special procedure, on proven misbehaviour or incapacity; salary and conditions of service determined by Parliament.

Art. 149: duties and powers over the accounts of the Union, the States and any other authority or body, as prescribed by law made by Parliament. The C&AG's (Duties, Powers and Conditions of Service) Act, 1971 defines them in detail.
Art. 150: on the C&AG's advice, the President prescribes the form in which Union and State accounts are kept.
Art. 151: C&AG reports on Central accounts go to the President, on State accounts to the Governor, who cause them to be laid before Parliament / the State Legislature.
DPC Act, 1971: term of 6 years or up to age 65, whichever is earlier; may resign by letter to the President.
The C&AG and the IAAD together form the Supreme Audit Institution (SAI) of India; senior functionaries representing the C&AG in a state are Accountants General.
P.mem: 148 Appoint · 149 Powers · 150 Form of accounts · 151 Reports laid.

P.label: C&AG audit reach
P.title: Organisations audited by the C&AG
P.law: The DPC Act, 1971 specifies the entities under the C&AG's audit, but the scope and extent of audit is determined by the C&AG himself.
notes: (1) All Union and State Government departments and offices, including Indian Railways and Posts and Telecommunications.
(2) Public commercial enterprises controlled by the Union and State governments, i.e. government companies and corporations.
(3) Non-commercial autonomous bodies and authorities owned or controlled by the Union or the States.
(4) Authorities and bodies substantially financed from Union or State revenues.
Because of these numerous audits every year, the C&AG issues a large number of audit reports.

P.label: Govt co. audit
P.title: Audit of government companies (commercial audit) and C&AG directions
P.short: C&AG appoints and directs the auditor
P.law: For companies where the Government's equity is 51% or more, the auditors are firms of Chartered Accountants appointed by the C&AG, who gives them directions on how the audit is to be conducted, is empowered to comment upon their audit reports, and has the right to conduct a supplementary audit and to cause a test audit by order.
notes: s.143(5) Companies Act, 2013: in a government company the C&AG may direct the auditor on the manner in which the accounts are to be audited; the auditor's report includes the directions, the action taken on them and their impact on the accounts (SM Test Your Understanding 2).

Typical directions: whether all accounting transactions go through the IT system; restructuring / waiver / write-off of loans due to inability to repay; whether scheme-specific grants and subsidies were properly accounted for and used.
Listing or disinvestment does not change this: while Government holds at least 51%, the company is a government company and the C&AG's role continues (SM TYK 5).

The accounts of selected government companies, with the statutory auditors' report, are reviewed by the C&AG through a supplementary audit; significant comments feed into the State report on government companies (SM chapter-opening case: depreciation comment, profit overstated by ₹20 crore).
P.mem: 51% → C&AG Appoints, Directs, Comments, Supplementary/Test audit.

P.label: s.139 / s.143 (Govt co.)
P.title: Audit of government companies: sections 139(5), 139(7), 139(8), 143(5), 143(6) and 143(7)
P.short: Appointment, directions, supplementary and test audit
P.law: s.139(5)/(7): statutory auditors of government companies are appointed or re-appointed by the C&AG (not by members at the AGM); remuneration is decided by the company within C&AG guidelines. s.143(5): the C&AG may direct the manner of audit; the auditor submits a copy of the report to the C&AG, including the directions, action taken and impact on the accounts. s.143(6)(a): within 60 days of receiving the audit report, the C&AG may conduct a supplementary audit. s.143(6)(b): the C&AG may comment upon or supplement the audit report; comments go to everyone entitled to the audited financial statements and are placed before the AGM with the audit report. s.143(7): the C&AG may by order cause a test audit; s.19A of the DPC Act, 1971 applies to its report.
notes: Casual vacancy in a government company's audit: filled by the C&AG within 30 days; if not, the Board fills it within the next 30 days (ICAI MTP Nov 2022 S-II MCQ 10).
The s.143(5) report is in addition to the auditor's reports under other clauses of s.143.
Source: ICAI MTP May 2023 S-I Q6(a). The current SM (Ch 15) states the same powers without section numbers: C&AG appoints, directs, comments, and may conduct supplementary and test audit.
P.mem: 139(5)/(7) Appoint · 143(5) Direct · 143(6)(a) Supplementary in 60 days · 143(6)(b) Comment · 143(7) Test audit.

P.label: Audit Boards
P.title: Audit Boards in commercial audit
P.law: A unique feature of IAAD audit is the constitution of Audit Boards for conducting comprehensive audit appraisals of the working of public sector enterprises in diverse sectors.
notes: They associate with them experts in the relevant disciplines.
They discuss findings with the enterprise's management and the controlling ministries/departments to obtain their viewpoints before finalisation.
Results are incorporated by the C&AG in his reports (see C&AG report, part (b)).
No separate legal entity: they work under the supervision and control of the C&AG.

P.label: PAC
P.title: Public Accounts Committee (PAC)
P.short: Money spent legally and as authorised
P.law: Audit reports and annual accounts automatically stand referred to specialised committees (PAC, Estimates Committee, COPU), because scrutiny by the whole Parliament would be impractical. The PAC must satisfy itself that: (i) moneys were disbursed legally on the service or purpose to which they were applied; (ii) the expenditure was authorised; (iii) re-appropriation was made in accordance with the provisions.
notes: It also examines the statement of accounts of autonomous and semi-autonomous bodies audited by the C&AG under the President's directions or a statute of Parliament.
Contrast: PAC controls government departments; COPU exercises the same control over public undertakings.

P.label: Estimates Committee
P.title: Estimates Committee
P.law: The Estimates Committee examines the estimates to: (i) report what economies, improvements in organisation, efficiency or administrative reform may be effected; (ii) suggest alternative policies; (iii) examine whether the money is well laid out within the limit; (iv) suggest the form in which estimates are presented to Parliament.
notes: It does not comment on a policy approved by Parliament; but where a policy is not giving the desired results or leads to waste, it brings this to the notice of the House.

P.label: COPU
P.title: Committee on Public Undertakings (COPU)
P.short: Examines PSU reports, accounts and C&AG reports
P.law: COPU exercises over public sector undertakings the same financial control that the PAC exercises over government departments. Its functions: (i) examine the reports and accounts of public undertakings; (ii) examine the reports of the C&AG on public undertakings; (iii) examine the autonomy and efficiency of public undertakings and whether they are managed on sound business principles and prudent commercial practices; (iv) other functions of the PAC and Estimates Committee not covered above, allotted by the Speaker.
notes: Its examination takes the form of a comprehensive appraisal of performance: policies, programmes and financial working.
Financial committees look not only at the individual irregularity but also at the system defects behind it and the correction needed.
Exam cue: a committee examining a PSU's physical and financial performance and pending action on C&AG findings → COPU (SM Test Your Understanding 1).

P.label: C&AG and committees
P.title: C&AG's role with the financial committees
P.law: The C&AG is recognised as the 'friend, philosopher and guide' of the financial committees of Parliament and the State Legislatures.
notes: His reports generally form the basis of the committees' work, though they may examine issues not in his reports.
He scrutinises the notes Ministries submit, and helps check the correctness of submissions and of facts and figures in draft reports.
Committees present reports with recommendations; Ministries report action taken; committees present Action Taken Reports.
For audit reports not discussed in detail, written answers are obtained from the Ministry and sometimes included in reports, so audit reports are not taken lightly.

P.label: Scope of PSU audit
P.title: Objective and scope of public enterprises audit
P.law: Audit of public enterprises is not restricted to financial and compliance audit; it extends to performance (efficiency, economy and effectiveness), propriety and comprehensive audit. Government audit covers (a) fiscal accountability: provision of funds, sanctions, compliance and propriety; and (b) managerial accountability: efficiency, economy and effectiveness (efficiency-cum-performance audit).
notes: (1) Not limited to financial and compliance audit. (2) Propriety of management decisions in sales, purchases, contracts. (3) Comprehensive audit: appraisal of whether objectives, value for money and targets were achieved.

(4) Decisions must be taken by the competent authority after examining all aspects (economic, technological, public interest), all relevant information and alternatives, consistent with the enterprise's aims.

(5) Audit helps Government and managements improve: brings out deficiencies and analyses causes. (6) Financial performance is linked with physical performance. (7) Fiscal and managerial accountability.
Efficiency-cum-performance audit: an objective examination of financial and operational performance oriented to identifying opportunities for greater efficiency, economy and effectiveness.

P.label: Elements of PSU audit
P.title: Basic elements: three parties; subject matter, criteria and subject matter information
P.law: Every PSU audit has: (a) three parties — auditor, responsible party and intended users; (b) subject matter, criteria and subject matter information; (c) a type of engagement — attestation or direct reporting.
notes: Auditor: the SAI India (C&AG + IAAD) and its personnel delegated to conduct audits.

Responsible party: set by constitutional or legislative arrangement; usually the auditable entity and TCWG. May be responsible for the subject matter information, for managing the subject matter, or for addressing recommendations.
Intended users: those for whom the auditor prepares the report.
Subject matter: information, condition or activity measured against criteria. Criteria: the benchmarks. Subject matter information: the outcome of that measurement.

P.label: Attestation vs direct
P.title: Attestation engagements and direct reporting engagements
P.law: In an attestation engagement the responsible party measures the subject matter against the criteria and presents the information; the auditor gathers evidence to express a conclusion on it. In a direct reporting engagement the auditor measures or evaluates the subject matter against the criteria.
notes: Financial audits are always attestation engagements (based on information presented by the responsible party).
Performance and compliance audits are generally direct reporting engagements.

P.label: Principles of PSU audit
P.title: Principles of PSU audits: general principles and audit-process principles
P.law: The principles are the general standards for SAI India's personnel, fundamental to all PSU audits, in two groups: I. General principles and II. Principles related to the audit process.
notes: General principles (8): ethics and independence; professional judgement, due care and scepticism; quality control; audit team management and skill; audit risk; materiality; documentation; communication.
Planning the audit: establish terms; understand the entity; risk assessment / problem analysis; identify fraud risks; develop an audit plan.
Conducting the audit: perform planned procedures to obtain evidence; evaluate evidence and draw conclusions.
Reporting and follow-up: prepare a report on the conclusions; follow up reported matters.

P.label: Financial audit
P.title: Financial audit by the C&AG
P.law: Financial audit is conducted to express an audit opinion on the financial statements and to enhance the confidence of intended users in them. The C&AG expresses an opinion on whether the financial statements are prepared, in all material respects, in accordance with the applicable financial reporting framework (for a fair presentation framework: presented fairly / true and fair view).
notes: Always an attestation engagement.

P.label: Compliance audit
P.title: Compliance audit: regularity and propriety
P.short: Does it comply with applicable criteria?
P.law: Compliance audit is the independent assessment of whether a given subject matter is in compliance with the applicable criteria: whether activities, financial transactions and information comply, in all material respects, with the regulatory and other rules governing the entity. It is concerned with (a) regularity — adherence to formal criteria from laws, regulations and agreements; and (b) propriety — observance of the general principles of sound financial management and the ethical conduct of public officials.
notes: Regularity is emphasised, but propriety is equally pertinent in the public sector.

Conducted (i) with the audit of financial statements, (ii) separately as individual compliance audits, or (iii) in combination with performance audit (non-compliance may then be a cause, explanation or consequence of the performance).

Compliance audit process: general principles and annual compliance audit plan → planning (objective and scope, strategy, subject matter and criteria, understanding entity and internal control, materiality, risk, procedures) → performing and gathering evidence (incl. non-compliance indicating suspected unlawful acts) → evaluating evidence and forming conclusions → reporting (include entity responses, follow up). Documentation, communication and quality control run throughout.

Exam cue: records don't match the rule in the law (e.g. buildings wrongly classified as flats, water charges under-collected) → compliance audit; for a State department the report goes to the Governor to be laid before the State Legislature under Art. 151 (SM TYK 9).
Chapter-opening case: insurance PSU issuing policies without actuarial valuation or required approvals → compliance audit.

P.label: Performance audit — 3Es
P.title: Performance audit: definition and the three Es
P.law: A performance audit is an objective and systematic examination of evidence to provide an independent assessment of the performance of a government organisation, programme, activity or function, to improve public accountability and facilitate decision-making. It examines whether decisions of the legislature or executive are efficiently and effectively prepared and implemented, and whether taxpayers have received value for money. It addresses economy, efficiency and effectiveness.
notes: Conducted by the C&AG (SAI) through subordinate IAAD offices, guided by C&AG manuals and auditing standards.

Economy: minimising the cost of resources for appropriate quantity and quality at the best price; resources acquired in due time. Questions: best prices for consultancy? cost of sickness absences? lowest transport costs? waste of resources?

Efficiency: the input-output ratio; output maximised for minimum input. Covers sound procurement, protection and maintenance of resources, efficient use of human and financial resources, optimum resources, efficient management and operating procedures, objectives met cost-effectively. Questions: cost per job created vs elsewhere? could project X be done better?

Effectiveness: extent to which objectives are achieved; intended vs actual impact. May assess whether objectives and means are proper, results achieved, whether impacts are due to the policy, factors inhibiting performance, overlap with other programmes, alternatives considered, management control system, compliance with laws, ways to work more effectively.

Performance audit cycle: strategic planning → planning individual audits → implementation (preliminary study, field audit, draft report to entity) → report approval → performance audit report → follow-up and impact assessment.
Chapter-opening case: steel PSU modernisation delayed, missing favourable market conditions → performance audit.
P.mem: Economy = cheap inputs; Efficiency = inputs→outputs; Effectiveness = outcomes vs objectives.

P.label: PA objectives
P.title: Objectives of performance audit
P.law: The objectives of performance auditing are evaluation of economy, efficiency and effectiveness of policy, programmes, organisation and management. It promotes accountability (helping TCWG and oversight bodies improve performance) and transparency (giving taxpayers and stakeholders insight into management and outcomes).
notes: It focuses on areas where it can add value with the greatest potential for development, and provides constructive incentives for responsible parties to act.

Regulations on Audit and Accounts: responsibility for measurable objectives, performance indicators and measurement systems rests with the Government departments / heads of entities, who must define intermediate and final outputs and outcomes, standardise unit cost of delivery and benchmark quality.

Minimum Wages Act example: know the industries and population covered; evaluate standard of living before and after; returns prescribed and obtained; 3Es in the welfare systems; coordination between labour department, EPF and ESI; gaps in the legal framework; actual compensation needed vs statutory minimum wage.
Exam cue: an audit that only checks expenses against public interest and accepted customs is propriety audit, not performance audit, so the C&AG may rightly reject it (SM TYK 7).
DBT schemes example objectives: proper planning to capture beneficiary data; steps against payment delays, pilferage and duplication; adequacy of DBT infrastructure and management (SM TYK 10).

P.label: PA planning steps
P.title: Planning for performance audit (steps A–I) and understanding the entity
P.law: Steps suggested for planning a performance audit: (A) understanding the entity/programme; (B) defining objectives and scope; (C) determining audit criteria; (D) deciding audit approach; (E) developing audit questions; (F) assessing audit team skills and need for outside expertise; (G) preparing the Audit Design Matrix; (H) establishing timetable and resources; (I) intimating the audit programme to the audited entity.
notes: (A) Understanding the entity is the starting point. Sources: (i) documents of the entity (policy files, annual reports, budgets, accounts, minutes, website, internal audit reports, MIS, RTI material); (ii) legislative documents (legislation, parliamentary questions and debates, PAC / COPU / Estimates Committee reports, MPs' letters); (iii) policy documents; (iv) academic or special research; (v) past audits; (vi) media coverage; (vii) special focus groups (Audit Advisory Committee, World Bank, RBI, NGOs).
(B) Objectives crisp and clear; scope limits the audit to significant issues (extent, timing, nature).
(E) Questions framed comprehensively, in a hierarchy. (F) Auditors need special aptitude; the Accountant General may use an expert but keeps full responsibility for the opinion.

(H) Selecting the team is the most vital component; the Accountant General is liable for timely completion; variations approved by the competent authority; build in time for translation and approvals.

(I) Intimate scope, team and tentative schedule well before commencement; record acknowledgement. Changes to objectives recorded and approved; programme kept flexible; significant refinements shared across teams at different locations.
Exam cue: team gathering entity records, legislative discussions, committee reports, prior audits, research and stakeholder inputs → stage (A), understanding the entity (RTP Nov 2026 Q18).
P.mem: U-O-C-A-Q-S-M-T-I: Understand, Objectives, Criteria, Approach, Questions, Skills, Matrix, Time, Intimate.

P.label: Audit criteria
P.title: Audit criteria and their sources
P.law: Audit criteria are the standards used to determine whether a programme meets or exceeds expectations; reasonable and attainable standards of performance against which economy, efficiency and effectiveness can be assessed. They give context for understanding the results.
notes: Sources: (i) procedure manuals of the entity; (ii) policies, standards, directives and guidelines; (iii) criteria used by the same or other entities in similar activities; (iv) independent expert opinion and know-how; (v) new or established scientific knowledge; (vi) general management and subject-matter literature and research papers.
DBT case: circulars, instructions, SOP manuals, scheme guidelines on identifying and authenticating beneficiaries, and subject literature (SM TYK 10).

P.label: PA approach & ADM
P.title: Audit approach methods and the Audit Design Matrix
P.law: No uniform approach applies to all performance audits. Methods include: (i) analysis of procedures; (ii) case studies; (iii) use of existing data; (iv) surveys; (v) analysis of results (output-input); (vi) quantitative analysis (with sampling where data is voluminous).
notes: Audit Design Matrix (ADM): a structured, focused design of the study, prepared from planning-stage knowledge, ideally for each audit objective. Columns: (1) audit objective, (2) audit questions, (3) audit criteria, (4) evidence, (5) data collection and analysis method.

P.label: Comprehensive audit
P.title: Comprehensive audit
P.law: The C&AG conducts an efficiency-cum-performance audit other than the field already covered by internal audit or the professional auditors, locating areas of weakness and extravagance for management. It combines financial, compliance and performance audit so a holistic assessment is possible: whether the undertaking fulfilled its objectives, obtained value for money and achieved targets.
notes: Areas: investment decisions, project formulation, organisational effectiveness, capacity utilisation, management of equipment and plant, production performance, use of materials, labour productivity, idle capacity, costs and prices, materials management, sales and credit control, budgetary and internal control systems.

Issues examined (a)–(j): capital cost vs approved cost and extravagance; planned output achieved or under-utilisation; planned rate of return achieved; soundness of project formulation and execution, effect on gestation period and cost; cost control and wastage; purchase policies and inventory pile-up; R&D and technology adoption; repairs and maintenance; effectiveness and economy of procedures; poor project planning.
Criteria: Bureau of Public Enterprises guidelines; industrial engineering and technical studies; standards of financial propriety.
Starting point: an audit programme based on the enterprise's setting-up decisions, objectives, operations, annual reports, budgets, board deliberations and earlier inspection reports.

P.label: Propriety audit
P.title: Propriety audit: definition and principles
P.short: Wasteful even though within the rules
P.law: Propriety audit is verification of transactions on the tests of public interest, commonly accepted customs and standards of conduct (E.L. Kohler). Auditors bring out cases of improper, avoidable or infructuous expenditure even though incurred in conformity with existing rules. Principles: (i) expenditure not prima facie more than the occasion demands, and every official exercises the vigilance a person of ordinary prudence would over his own money; (ii) no authority sanctions expenditure to its own advantage; (iii) funds not used for the benefit of a particular person or group; (iv) apart from agreed remuneration, no other avenue to indirectly benefit management, employees and others.
notes: The tests boil down to economy, efficiency and faithfulness; emphasis shifts from vouchers to the substance of transactions.
Examples: a building for a telephone exchange not used for it = infructuous; a school used five years after completion = avoidable expenditure.
Enforcing economy is the executive's responsibility; audit brings wastefulness to the notice of the proper authorities.
See also Propriety audit — auditor's functions and subjectivity.

P.label: Propriety — issues
P.title: Propriety audit: auditor's functions and the problem of subjectivity
P.law: In propriety audit the auditor should see that: expenditure is properly planned; the size and channels of expenditure are rightful and expected to give maximum results; expenditure is likely to give optimum results; whether a substitute plan could improve operations and returns; and management's actions are conducive to public interest and standards of conduct.
notes: Issue: 'propriety' is a moral term; verifiable audit propositions are hard to formulate, so there is inherent subjectivity. The C&AG has developed norms of propriety for public expenditure.
Government norms do not automatically apply to the private sector; if each entity framed its own propriety norms, subjectivity would reduce.
Judge decisions in the circumstances when they were taken, not on hindsight; reconstruct those circumstances. Air travel is not wasteful unless rail was feasible with the same result.
Over-subjective judgment would dampen management initiative and make propriety audit counter-productive.

P.label: C&AG report
P.title: Audit report of the C&AG on PSUs
P.law: The C&AG's reports on PSUs are presented to Parliament in parts: (a) introduction with a general review of working results of government companies, deemed government companies and corporations; (b) results of comprehensive appraisals by the Audit Board; (c) resume of company auditors' reports under the C&AG's directions and comments on the accounts; (d) significant results of audit of undertakings not taken up for appraisal by the Audit Board.
notes: For certain specified States the C&AG submits a separate audit report (commercial) to the legislature; for other States / UTs with legislature there is a commercial chapter in the main report.

State reports contain appraisals of selected companies, important instances of financial irregularity, wasteful expenditure, system deficiencies noticed by statutory auditors, and a general review of working results.
Reports go to the President / Governor under Art. 151.

Q.q:
The objectives of audit in connection with a State Electricity Distribution Company were to ascertain whether: (i) the total cost of providing electricity is being recovered by timely submissions to the State Electricity Regulatory Commission; (ii) tariff orders, sales circulars and sales instructions were issued timely, without ambiguity, and implemented in time; (iii) metering, billing and collection was managed efficiently and effectively; (iv) monitoring and internal controls were efficient.

What kind of audit is this? Prepare two sample observations which could be part of the audit report.
Q.a:
Type: This is a performance audit: every objective asks whether the company recovers costs and runs billing, collection and controls efficiently and effectively.

Sample observation (i) — Non-replacement of defective/burnt meters: a large number of meters, much in excess of the permitted limit of 1% of total meters, were defective and not replaced within the stipulated 1 month. This led to billing on an average basis for several months, which could cause losses, administrative hassles and disputes with consumers.

Sample observation (ii) — Under-charging of meter rent: the Schedule of Charges requires meter rent of ₹30 per month (single phase) and ₹40 per month (three phase). The company short-charged meter rent of ₹60 lakh from 3 lakh consumers in 5 lakh bills during the period.

Also asked (ICAI): RTP May 2022 Q21.
Q.trap: Calling it a compliance audit because tariff orders are involved. The objectives test efficiency and effectiveness of operations, which is performance audit.

Q.q:
PGC & Associates are statutory auditors of BNPC Limited, a PSU in the power sector building large thermal power stations. One of the financial committees of Parliament has decided to examine its physical and financial performance. It has also examined the C&AG's audit findings on which action is yet to be taken by the PSU, and proposes to include in its report the company's performance in various operational matters.

Which financial committee of Parliament deals with such matters? Outline its main functions.
Q.a:
Committee: the Committee on Public Undertakings (COPU).

Functions: (i) to examine the reports and accounts of public undertakings; (ii) to examine the reports of the C&AG on public undertakings; (iii) to examine the autonomy and efficiency of public undertakings and whether they are managed in accordance with sound business principles and prudent commercial practices; (iv) to exercise such other functions of the PAC and the Estimates Committee as are not covered above and are allotted by the Speaker.

Conclusion: COPU's examination takes the form of a comprehensive appraisal of the undertaking's performance, including its policies, programmes and financial working, which is exactly what is described.

Also asked (ICAI): MTP May 2025 S-I Q6(c) OR (MBPC Ltd, 4 marks).
Q.trap: Answering PAC. The PAC deals with government departments; the equivalent committee for public undertakings is COPU.

Q.q:
PS & Associates are statutory auditors of a Central Government owned company. They were required to examine the following areas mandatorily, give specific replies and state the impact on the financial statements in their audit report:

1. Whether the company processes all accounting transactions through its IT system; if not, the implications on the integrity of accounts and the financial implications.
2. Whether any existing loan was restructured, or debts / loans / interest waived or written off by a lender because of the company's inability to repay; the financial impact and whether properly accounted for.
3. Whether funds (grants/subsidy) received or receivable for specific schemes from the Central Government or its agencies were properly accounted for and used as per their terms; list cases of deviation.

Can you determine the likely nature of such responsibility thrust upon the auditors of this PSU?
Q.a:
Provision: These areas are likely to be directions issued by the C&AG under section 143(5) of the Companies Act, 2013.

Analysis: Under section 143(5), in the case of a government company the C&AG has the power to direct the auditor on the manner in which the company's accounts are to be audited. The auditor's report must include the directions, if any, issued by the C&AG, the action taken on them and their impact on the accounts and financial statements of the company.

Conclusion: The responsibility arises from C&AG directions under s.143(5); the auditors must report on each area and its impact on the financial statements.
Q.trap: Treating these as CARO clauses. The mandatory, company-specific questions set for a government company's auditor are s.143(5) directions.

Q.q: The reports of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India on the audit of PSUs are presented to the Parliament and to various state legislatures to facilitate a proper consideration. Enumerate the contents of the Audit Report presented by the C&AG.
Q.a:
Contents (para 9): the reports are presented in several parts: (a) an introduction containing a general review of the working results of government companies, deemed government companies and corporations; (b) results of comprehensive appraisals of selected undertakings conducted by the Audit Board; (c) a resume of the company auditors' reports submitted under the directions issued by the C&AG and of comments on the accounts of government companies; and (d) significant results of audit of undertakings not taken up for appraisal by the Audit Board.

For certain specified States the C&AG submits a separate audit report (commercial) to the legislature; for other States / UTs with legislature there is a commercial chapter in the main audit report. State reports contain appraisals of selected companies, important instances of financial irregularities, wasteful expenditure and system deficiencies noticed by statutory auditors, and a general review of working results.

Also asked (ICAI): PYQ Dec 2021 Q3(a), 5 marks.

Q.q: ABG & Co., a Chartered Accountant firm, has been appointed by the C&AG for performance audit of a Sugar Industry. What factors should ABG & Co. consider while planning a performance audit of the Sugar Industry?
Q.a:
Factors (para 6.2):

  • Understanding the entity/programme: the starting point, using entity documents, legislative and policy documents, research, past audits, media coverage and special focus groups.
  • Defining objectives and scope: crisp, clear objectives; scope limited to significant issues.
  • Determining audit criteria: reasonable and attainable standards (procedure manuals, guidelines, comparable entities, expert opinion, scientific knowledge, literature).
  • Deciding the audit approach: analysis of procedures, case studies, existing data, surveys, analysis of results, quantitative analysis.
  • Developing audit questions in a hierarchy.
  • Assessing team skills and whether outside expertise is needed; responsibility for the opinion stays with the auditor.
  • Preparing the Audit Design Matrix: objective, questions, criteria, evidence, data collection and analysis method.
  • Establishing timetable and resources.
  • Intimating the audit programme (scope, team, schedule) to the entity before commencement.

Q.q: Sunlight Limited is a public sector undertaking producing electricity from solar power. It commissioned a new project near Goa with a new technology at a cost of ₹5,750 crore. The project saw delay in commencement and cost overrun. State the matters that a Comprehensive Audit by the C&AG may cover in reporting on the performance and efficiency of this project.
Q.a:
Comprehensive audit (para 7) combines financial, compliance and performance audit into a holistic assessment of whether the project met its objectives and gave value for money. For Sunlight's project it may examine:

  • How the overall capital cost (₹5,750 crore) compares with the approved planned cost; reasons for the overrun; any extravagance or unnecessary expenditure.
  • Whether planned production/output has been achieved; under-utilisation of installed capacity and its causes.
  • Whether the planned rate of return has been achieved.
  • Whether project formulation and execution systems are sound, and the effect of inadequacies on the gestation period (the delay) and capital cost.
  • Adequacy of cost control; inefficiencies and wastage in materials.
  • Adequacy of purchase policies; piling up of inventory, stores and spares.
  • R&D and performance in adopting the new technology to improve profits and reduce costs.
  • Adequacy of the repairs and maintenance system; whether procedures are effective and economical; any poor or inefficient project planning.

Also asked (ICAI): PYQ Nov 2023 Q5(a); MTP Nov 2022 S-I Q6(a); MTP Dec 2021 S-II Q6(a).
Q.trap: Listing only cost overrun. The answer should cover the full list of comprehensive-audit issues and tie them to the delay and overrun.

Q.q: "A performance audit is an objective and systematic examination of evidence for the purpose of providing an independent assessment of the performance of a government organization, program, activity, or function in order to provide information to improve public accountability and facilitate decision-making by parties with responsibility to oversee or initiate corrective action." Briefly discuss the issues addressed by Performance Audits conducted in accordance with the guidelines issued by the C&AG.
Q.a:
Issues addressed (para 6): economy, efficiency and effectiveness.

Economy: minimising the cost of resources used, having regard to appropriate quantity and quality, at the best price; whether resources were acquired in due time, in appropriate quantity and quality at the best price.

Efficiency: the input-output ratio; output maximised at minimum input. It covers sound procurement, protection and maintenance of resources, efficient use of human and financial resources, optimum resources for timely delivery, efficient management and operating procedures, and meeting objectives cost-effectively.

Effectiveness: the extent to which objectives are achieved and the relationship between intended and actual impact: whether objectives and means are proper, the extent of results achieved, whether impacts are due to the policy, factors inhibiting performance, overlaps with other programmes, alternatives considered, adequacy of management control systems, compliance with laws, and ways to make programmes more effective.

Q.q: BT Ltd., a company wholly owned by the Central Government, was disinvested during the previous year, resulting in 40% of the shares being held by the public. The shares were listed on the BSE and all listing requirements apply. Sam, the FM, believes that since the company is now subject to stringent control by BSE and the markets, the auditing requirements of a private-sector company under the Companies Act, 2013 apply and the C&AG will have no role. Comment.
Q.a:
Provision: Section 2(45) of the Companies Act, 2013 defines a government company as one in which not less than 51% of the paid-up share capital is held by the Central Government, any State Government(s), or partly by both, and includes a subsidiary of such a company. The auditors of government companies are firms of Chartered Accountants appointed by the C&AG, who directs the manner of audit.

Analysis: After disinvestment the Government still holds 60%, so BT Ltd. remains a government company. Listing on a stock exchange is irrelevant to this status.

Conclusion: Sam's opinion is not correct; the C&AG continues to appoint and direct the auditors of BT Ltd.

Also asked (ICAI): RTP May 2023 Q21 (Siddha Ltd, 40% disinvested and listed on BSE).
Q.trap: Being swayed by the listing. Only the Government shareholding (≥ 51%) decides government-company status.

Q.q: You have been appointed as auditor of AKY Ltd. Having determined the audit objectives, you have been requested to draft audit criteria. What are the sources that you will use while doing the task?
Q.a:
Audit criteria (para 6.2(C)) are reasonable and attainable standards of performance against which economy, efficiency and effectiveness can be assessed. Sources:

  • procedure manuals of the entity;
  • policies, standards, directives and guidelines;
  • criteria used by the same or other entities in similar activities or programmes;
  • independent expert opinion and know-how;
  • new or established scientific knowledge and other reliable information;
  • general management and subject-matter literature and research papers.

Also asked (ICAI): MTP Dec 2021 S-I Q6(a) (ARHAM Ltd).

Q.q: The Comptroller & Auditor General appointed Verma & Associates, a chartered accountant firm, to conduct a Performance Audit of MAP Ltd., a PSU of the Government of India. The firm conducted the audit with a view to checking that all the expenses of the unit are in conformity with public interest and publicly accepted customs. The audit report submitted was rejected by the C&AG. Give your opinion on the action of the C&AG.
Q.a:
Provision: A performance audit is an objective and systematic examination of evidence to provide an independent assessment of the performance of a government organisation, programme, activity or function. Its objectives are evaluation of the economy, efficiency and effectiveness of policy, programmes, organisation and management; it promotes accountability and transparency. Responsibility for measurable objectives and performance indicators rests with the departments / heads of entities.

Analysis: Verma & Associates only checked whether expenses conform to public interest and publicly accepted customs. That is a propriety test, not an evaluation of economy, efficiency and effectiveness.

Conclusion: The audit done is not a performance audit in all aspects, so the C&AG's rejection of the report is in order.
Q.trap: Saying public interest is part of performance audit so the report is fine. Checking expenses against public interest and customs is the propriety test; performance audit must evaluate the 3Es.

Q.q:
The objectives of audit in connection with a State Electricity Distribution Company were to ascertain whether: (i) total cost of providing electricity is being recovered by timely submissions to the State Electricity Regulatory Commission; (ii) tariff orders, sales circulars and sales instructions were issued timely, without ambiguity, and implemented in time; (iii) metering, billing and collection was managed efficiently and effectively; (iv) monitoring and internal controls were efficient.

What kind of audit is referred to? Also briefly discuss the steps suggested to the auditors for planning such an audit.
Q.a:
Type: In view of the objectives, this is a performance audit.

Planning steps (para 6.2): (A) understanding the entity/programme; (B) defining the objectives and scope of audit; (C) determining audit criteria; (D) deciding the audit approach; (E) developing audit questions; (F) assessing audit team skills and whether outside expertise is required; (G) preparing the Audit Design Matrix; (H) establishing the timetable and resources; (I) intimating the audit programme to the audited entity. Explain each briefly.

Also asked (ICAI): RTP May 2022 Q21 (full planning steps).

Q.q:
During the audit of a state government department, the office of the C&AG observed that the state law defined a "flat" on two criteria: dwelling units exceeding a threshold, and buildings with total area exceeding a threshold. The department's database had no column for building area, so some buildings were classified as flats although they had fewer dwelling units than the threshold. Physical verification confirmed they were wrongly classified, resulting in under-collection of water charges.

Identify the type and nature of audit performed by the office of the C&AG. To whom was the report of such audit likely to have been submitted?
Q.a:
Type: a compliance audit: an independent assessment of whether a subject matter complies with the applicable criteria, i.e. whether activities, financial transactions and information comply, in all material respects, with the rules governing the entity. It is concerned with regularity (adherence to laws, regulations and agreements) and propriety (sound financial management and ethical conduct of officials).

Report: under Article 151, C&AG reports on State accounts are submitted to the Governor, who causes them to be laid before the State Legislative Assembly. As this relates to a State department, the report would have gone to the Governor of the State.
Q.trap: Calling it a performance audit because revenue was lost. The test was conformity with the statutory definition of a flat: compliance audit.

Q.q:
Direct Benefit Transfer (DBT) is a major reform to deliver benefits like wage payments, fuel subsidies and food grain subsidies directly into beneficiaries' bank accounts, removing leakages and enhancing financial inclusion. The office of the C&AG is likely to undertake a performance audit, for a block of years in a state, of some selected social security pension schemes and scholarship schemes under DBT.

What are likely to be the objectives of such a performance audit? Explain the meaning of "audit criteria" and discuss how these can be determined in this case.
Q.a:
Likely objectives:

  • whether proper planning and processes were in place to capture beneficiary data under the schemes;
  • whether steps were taken to implement DBT so as to prevent payment delays to intended beneficiaries, pilferage and duplication;
  • whether the infrastructure, organisation and management of DBT were adequate and effective.

Audit criteria are standards used to determine whether a programme meets or exceeds expectations; reasonable and attainable standards against which economy, efficiency and effectiveness are assessed, giving context to the results.

Determination here: documents issued by the Government of India and the state government such as circulars, instructions, standard operating procedure manuals, scheme guidelines on identification and authentication of beneficiaries, and general management and subject-matter literature.

Also asked (ICAI): MTP May 2024 S-I Q5(b), verbatim.

Q.q:
CA Smita joined the Indian Audit and Accounts Service. (1) In a test audit of an insurance PSU she found policies issued to mobile-handset sellers (free insurance tied to buying an app) without any actuarial valuation or required approvals, causing losses from non-compliant underwriting. (2) She was part of a team auditing a government steel company's modernisation: projects were delayed and not completed in time, so the company missed favourable market conditions. (3) Later she compiled a report on State government companies, including a C&AG comment that improper depreciation in a state power company's financial statements overstated profits by ₹20 crore.

Identify the nature of audit or audit work in each of (1), (2) and (3).
Q.a:
(1) Compliance audit: the team checked whether the PSU complied with regulatory norms for issuing insurance policies (the SM calls it a compliance audit). Missing actuarial valuation and approvals are non-compliances with the applicable criteria.

(2) Performance audit: deficiencies in project planning, tender finalisation and execution, and delays that lost market opportunities, go to economy, efficiency and effectiveness.

(3) Supplementary audit by the C&AG of a government company's financial statements: the C&AG may comment on the statutory auditor's report, and significant comments (profit overstated by ₹20 crore) feed into the report on the financial performance of State government companies.
Q.trap: Calling (1) a propriety audit because of losses. The test was conformity with regulatory norms for issuing policies, so it is a compliance audit.

Q.q:
The Comptroller and Auditor General has initiated a performance audit of a large government programme aimed at rural infrastructure development. The audit team has been assigned the task of planning the audit. The programme is implemented across multiple ministries, has been operational for several years, and has attracted attention in parliamentary discussions and media reports due to concerns about its efficiency and outcomes.

The audit team is considering sources such as internal records of the implementing agencies, legislative discussions, reports of committees, prior audit findings, independent research studies and inputs from stakeholders to develop a comprehensive understanding of the programme before finalising the audit plan.

Identify the stage of the performance audit process represented in the above scenario. Further discuss how the various sources of information assist the audit team in developing an in-depth understanding of the entity/programme for effective audit planning.
Q.a:
Stage: the initial stage of planning a performance audit, understanding the entity/programme. It is the starting point for planning an individual performance audit.

Sources for understanding the entity:

  • Documents of the entity: administration and functions, policy files, annual reports, budget documents, accounts, minutes, website information, internal audit reports, electronic databases and MIS reports, RTI material.
  • Legislative documents: legislation, parliamentary questions and debates, reports of the PAC, COPU and Estimates Committee, and letters from Members of Parliament.
  • Policy documents: documents of the Planning Commission, Ministry of Finance, etc.
  • Academic or special research: independent evaluations, academic research and similar work by other governments and SAIs.
  • Past audits: past financial and performance audits are a major source of information.
  • Media coverage: systematic, regular documentation of print and electronic media.
  • Special focus groups: Audit Advisory Committee concerns, World Bank and RBI reports, reports by special interest groups and NGOs.
Q.trap: Naming the stage as 'determining audit criteria' or 'developing audit questions'. Gathering background from many sources before finalising the plan is understanding the entity.

Q.q:
RST Ltd., a public sector company engaged in power generation, has recently completed five years of operations. The Board has requested an audit to evaluate not only the accuracy of its financial statements but also the efficiency of operations, adequacy of internal controls and overall performance. Preliminary review shows: several projects had cost overruns against approved budgets; some plants operate below installed capacity; raw material and fuel consumption exceed standard norms, and inventory management appears weak.

Identify the type of audit suitable in this scenario and suggest the key issues that the auditors should examine.
Q.a:
Type: a Comprehensive Audit (efficiency-cum-performance audit). It combines aspects of financial, compliance and performance audits so that a holistic assessment is possible; the areas covered vary with the nature, objectives and operations of the enterprise.

Issues to examine: (a) overall capital cost vs approved planned cost; substantial increases, extravagance or unnecessary expenditure; (b) whether planned production/outputs were achieved; under-utilisation of installed capacity and its causes; (c) whether the planned rate of return was achieved; (d) soundness of project formulation and execution and the effect on gestation period and capital cost; (e) adequacy of cost control; inefficiencies and wastage in raw material consumption; (f) adequacy of purchase policies; piling up of inventory and redundancy in stores and spares; (g) R&D and adoption of new processes and technologies; (h) adequacy of repairs and maintenance; (i) whether procedures are effective and economical; (j) poor, insufficient or inefficient project planning.
Q.trap: Answering 'performance audit' only. The Board wants accuracy of financial statements plus efficiency, controls and overall performance together, which is comprehensive audit.

Q.q: The C&AG appointed Sharma & Associates, a firm of Chartered Accountants, to conduct a performance audit of NAL Ltd., a public sector undertaking of the Government of India. The audit was conducted with the objective of examining whether all expenses of the unit were in conformity with public interest and accepted customs. The audit report submitted by the firm was rejected by the C&AG. Is the action of the C&AG justified?
Q.a:
Provision: A performance audit is an objective and systematic examination of evidence to provide an independent assessment of the performance of a government organisation, programme, activity or function, to improve public accountability and facilitate decision-making. It is conducted by the C&AG through IAAD offices guided by C&AG manuals and standards. Its objectives are evaluation of economy, efficiency and effectiveness of policy, programmes, organisation and management; it promotes accountability and transparency. Responsibility for measurable objectives, performance indicators and measurement systems rests with government departments / heads of entities.

Analysis: The firm only checked that expenses conform to public interest and publicly accepted customs. That is not a performance audit.

Conclusion: The C&AG's rejection of the report is in order, because merely checking expenses against public interest and accepted customs is not performance audit in all aspects.
Q.trap: Same as SM TYK 7: public interest and accepted customs is the propriety test, not the 3Es.

Q.q:
(Integrated case) Reliant & Co. was appointed to conduct the audit of a State Housing Department. The office of the C&AG found that the state law defined a 'flat' by number of dwelling units and total building area, but the database had no column for area; buildings were wrongly classified as flats and water charges were under-collected.

The report of audit of the State Housing Department by the C&AG is likely to be submitted to:
opts: The Board of the Authority directly
The Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs
Q.why: Under Article 151, C&AG reports on the accounts of a State go to the Governor, who causes them to be laid before the State Legislature. (ICAI's key gives only the option; explanation from SM para 2 / TYK 9.)
Q.a: Answer: (b) The Governor of the State (Article 151).

Q.q:
During the audit of a state government department, the office of the C&AG observed that the state law defined a "flat" on two criteria: dwelling units exceeding a threshold, and buildings with total area exceeding a threshold. The database had no column for building area, so some buildings were classified as flats although they had fewer dwelling units than the threshold. Physical verification confirmed the wrong classification, resulting in under-collection of water charges.

Identify the type and nature of audit performed by the office of the C&AG, and to whom the report was likely to have been submitted.
Q.a:
Type: a Compliance Audit performed by the office of the C&AG: an independent assessment of whether a subject matter complies with the applicable criteria, i.e. whether activities, financial transactions and information comply in all material respects with the rules governing the entity. It is concerned with (i) regularity (adherence to laws, regulations and agreements) and (ii) propriety (sound financial management and ethical conduct of public officials); regularity is emphasised, but propriety is equally pertinent in the public sector.

Report: under Article 151, C&AG reports on Central/State accounts go to the President/Governor, who lay them before Parliament/State Legislature. As this is a State department, the report was likely submitted to the Governor of the State, to be laid before the State Legislative Assembly.

Also asked: SM TYK 9; RTP Jan 2026 MCQ 3.
Q.trap: Answering 'performance audit' because revenue was lost. The test was conformity with the statutory definition: compliance audit.

Q.q: The C&AG appointed Rajni & Associates to conduct a performance audit of LBC Ltd., a PSU under the Government of India. The firm examined whether the expenses incurred were in conformity with public interest and publicly accepted customs. The audit report was rejected by the C&AG. Give your opinion on the action of the C&AG.
Q.a:
The firm checked whether expenses conform to public interest and publicly accepted customs, which is not performance audit.

Performance audit is an objective and systematic examination of evidence to provide an independent assessment of the performance of a government organisation, programme, activity or function, to improve public accountability and facilitate decision-making. It is conducted by the C&AG through IAAD offices guided by C&AG manuals and standards. Its objectives are evaluation of economy, efficiency and effectiveness; it promotes accountability and transparency and focuses where it can add most value. Responsibility for measurable objectives and performance indicators rests with the departments / heads of entities.

Conclusion: the C&AG's rejection of the report is in order, as merely checking expenses against public interest and accepted customs is not performance audit in all aspects.

Also asked (ICAI): MTP May 2023 S-II Q6(a) (OM Ltd); RTP Jan 2026 Q17; RTP May 2024 Q16; RTP Nov 2022 Q22; SM TYK 7.
Q.trap: Public interest and accepted customs is the propriety test, not the 3Es.

Q.q: TYU & Associates LLP, appointed by the C&AG for a planned performance audit of Heavy Electricals Corporation (a PSU), is asked to prepare an Audit Design Matrix for each audit objective. Which one of the following is not part of the ADM?
Q.why: ADM columns: audit objective, audit questions, audit criteria, evidence, data collection and analysis method. (ICAI key: (b). Same question as PYQ Nov 2024 MCQ 11.)
Q.a: Answer: (b) Audit programme.

Q.q:
The C&AG has appointed a Chartered Accountant firm to conduct the comprehensive audit of Saras Company Limited, a listed government company handling a major metropolitan railway project, for the period ending 31-03-2024. Project A involved laying 130 km of railway line. The firm reviewed the internal audit report, which reported that Current liabilities and Capital work in progress of Project A were understated by ₹75.32 crore.

What key aspects should the firm focus on while conducting the comprehensive audit of Saras Company Limited?
Q.a:
Matters for the comprehensive audit:

  • (i) overall capital cost vs approved planned costs; substantial increases; extravagance or unnecessary expenditure;
  • (ii) whether accepted production/operational outputs were achieved; under-utilisation of capacity or shortfall and its cause;
  • (iii) whether the planned rate of return was achieved;
  • (iv) soundness of project formulation and execution; effect on gestation period and capital cost;
  • (v) adequacy of cost control; inefficiencies and wastage in raw materials;
  • (vi) adequacy of purchase policies; inventory pile-up and redundant stores and spares;
  • (vii) R&D and adoption of new processes and technologies;
  • (viii) adequacy of repairs and maintenance;
  • (ix) whether procedures are effective and economical;
  • (x) poor, insufficient or inefficient project planning.
Q.trap: Being distracted by the ₹75.32 crore understatement into a financial-audit answer. The question asks for comprehensive-audit aspects.

Q.q: "The C&AG may direct the appointed auditor about the manner in which the accounts of the Government Company are required to be audited and thereupon the auditor so appointed shall submit a copy of the audit report to the Comptroller and Auditor-General of India." What are the relevant sections of the Companies Act, 2013 and the steps involved in the audit of Government Companies?
Q.a:
(i) Appointment, s.139(5) and 139(7) read with s.143(5): statutory auditors of government companies are appointed or re-appointed by the C&AG, a departure from private companies where members decide at the AGM. Remuneration is left to the company, based on C&AG guidelines.

(ii) Directions, s.143(5): the C&AG may direct the manner of audit; the auditor submits a copy of the report to the C&AG, including the directions, action taken and impact on the accounts and financial statements. This report is in addition to reports under other clauses of s.143.

(iii) Supplementary audit, s.143(6)(a): within 60 days from receipt of the audit report, the C&AG may conduct a supplementary audit by persons he authorises, and require information or additional information as he directs.

(iv) Comments, s.143(6)(b): C&AG comments upon or supplementing the audit report are sent by the company to every person entitled to copies of the audited financial statements under s.136(1) and placed before the AGM with the audit report.

(v) Test audit, s.143(7): the C&AG may, if necessary, by order cause a test audit of a company covered by s.139(5) or (7); s.19A of the C&AG's (DPC) Act, 1971 applies to its report.
Q.trap: Forgetting the 60-day limit for supplementary audit, or saying the members appoint the auditor.

Q.q: You are auditing the IT department of a PSU with a checklist containing questions such as: Are separate user-names and passwords assigned to individual users? Are periodical changes of passwords ensured? Are external (offsite) data backups maintained outside the premises? The type of audit being conducted is likely to be:
Q.why: ICAI's key: (a). Comprehensive audit covers the enterprise's systems, including budgetary and internal control systems, beyond the financial statements; an IT-controls checklist fits that holistic review. (ICAI gives no explanation; this reasoning is from SM para 7.)
Q.a: Answer: (a) Comprehensive audit (ICAI key).

Q.q: CA Ansh, auditor of Rajul Ltd. (Government of Puducherry holds 49% and a Central PSU holds 51%), resigned on 1 June 2021. The Board appointed CA Babu on 16 June 2021. A shareholder contends the appointment is invalid. Is the contention right?
opts: No. The appointment is valid since it is made within 30 days of the resignation.
Yes. Within 30 days it should have been made by the shareholders; the Board can appoint only if no auditor is appointed beyond 60 days.
Yes. Within 30 days it should have been made by the C&AG; the Board can appoint only if no auditor is appointed even beyond 30 days.
Yes. Within 30 days it should have been made by the shareholders; the Board can appoint only if no auditor is appointed beyond 30 days.
Q.why: Rajul Ltd. is a government company (Puducherry 49% + a government company's 51%). A casual vacancy in a government company is filled by the C&AG within 30 days; only if the C&AG fails to do so does the Board fill it within the next 30 days. (ICAI key: (c).)
Q.a: Answer: (c)

Q.q: A state government owned PSU was setting up a thermal power plant. The C&AG, in its audit report, pointed out delay in completion of work due to failure to decide on the type of water treatment in the cooling plant on time, besides frequent changes in lay-out and re-testing of soil by the company. What kind of audit is referred to? Describe the methods which could be used in conducting such audits.
Q.a:
Type: Performance audit: an objective and systematic examination of evidence to provide an independent assessment of the performance of a government organisation, programme, activity or function, to improve public accountability and facilitate decision-making.

Methods:

  • (i) Analysis of procedures: review of systems for planning, conducting, checking and monitoring the activity (financial reports, budgets, programme guidelines, procedure manuals).
  • (ii) Case studies: descriptive analysis of an entity, scheme or programme; a particular issue within the whole area.
  • (iii) Use of existing data: data held by management and other sources, tested for correctness and completeness.
  • (iv) Surveys: collecting information from members of a population on predetermined parameters.
  • (v) Analysis of results: actual output-input analysis to determine efficiency.
  • (vi) Quantitative analysis: financial or programme data; sampling where volume is high.
Q.trap: Answering 'comprehensive audit' because it is a project. The C&AG's point is delay and decision-making in execution; ICAI treats it as performance audit and asks for its methods.

Q.q: With respect to audit of public sector undertakings, which of the following relates to propriety audit?
opts: Assessing whether activities, financial transactions and information comply in all material aspects with the regulatory and other authorities governing the entity
Focusing on areas where it can add value with the greatest potential for development, providing constructive incentives to responsible parties
An audit in which the C&AG does not cover again the field already covered, but conducts an appraisal or efficiency-cum-performance audit
Verification of transactions on the tests of public interest, commonly accepted customs and standards of conduct, examining management decisions in sales, purchases, contracts, etc.
Q.why: (d) is propriety audit. (a) is compliance audit, (b) is performance audit, (c) is comprehensive audit. (ICAI key: (d).)
Q.a: Answer: (d)

Q.q: The reports of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India on the audit of PSUs are presented to the Parliament and to various state legislatures to facilitate a proper consideration. Enumerate the contents of the Audit Report presented by the C&AG.
Q.a:
The reports are presented to Parliament in several parts: (i) an introduction containing a general review of the working results of Government companies, deemed Government companies and corporations; (ii) results of comprehensive appraisals of selected undertakings conducted by the Audit Board; (iii) resume of the company auditors' reports submitted under the C&AG's directions and of comments on the accounts of Government companies; and (iv) significant results of audit of undertakings not taken up for appraisal by the Audit Board.

For certain specified States, the C&AG submits a separate audit report (commercial) to the legislature; for other States/UTs with legislature there is a commercial chapter in the main audit report. State reports contain appraisal results of selected companies/corporations, important instances of financial irregularities, wasteful expenditure, system deficiencies noticed by statutory auditors, and a general review of working results.

Same as SM TYK 1.

Q.q:
The C&AG appointed M/s VR & Associates to audit Sunshine Ltd., a PSU under the Government of India. Sunshine Ltd. proposed a solar panel manufacturing project in North Gujarat at an estimated cost of ₹5,750 crore, including ₹2,000 crore earmarked for R&D. All approvals, documentation and statutory requirements were duly complied with, but the C&AG was concerned that the proposed R&D expenditure appeared wasteful and lacking justification on the tests of public interest, as several established companies were already engaged in similar activities in that region.

Identify the type of audit that the C&AG expects M/s VR & Associates to conduct. Also explain the principles of this audit.
Q.a:
Type: Propriety audit, because the C&AG's concern is that the ₹2,000 crore R&D spend appears wasteful and unjustified on the test of public interest, even though all rules were complied with. Propriety audit stands for verification of transactions on the tests of public interest, commonly accepted customs and standards of conduct.

Principles (transactions, particularly expenditure, must conform to them):

  • (i) expenditure is not prima facie more than the occasion demands, and every official exercises the vigilance a person of ordinary prudence would over his own money;
  • (ii) the sanctioning authority does not pass an order that directly or indirectly accrues to its own advantage;
  • (iii) funds are not utilised for the benefit of a particular person or group of persons;
  • (iv) apart from agreed remuneration or reward, no other avenue is kept open to indirectly benefit management personnel, employees and others.
Q.trap: 'All approvals and statutory requirements complied with' points away from compliance audit: the question is whether the spend is wasteful despite being within the rules, which is propriety.

Q.q: Sonar Limited is a public sector undertaking producing electricity from solar power. It commissioned a new project near Mumbai with new technology at a cost of ₹4,750 crore. The project saw delays in commencement and cost overruns. State ANY FIVE matters that a Comprehensive Audit by the C&AG may cover in reporting on the performance and efficiency of this project.
Q.a:
Areas covered in comprehensive audit vary with the enterprise; in general they are investment decisions, project formulation, organisational effectiveness, capacity utilisation, management of plant, production performance, use of materials, labour productivity, idle capacity, costs and prices, materials management, sales and credit control, budgetary and internal control systems.

Matters examined (any five):

  • (1) overall capital cost vs approved planned cost; substantial increases; extravagance or unnecessary expenditure;
  • (2) planned production/outputs achieved; under-utilisation of installed capacity and its cause;
  • (3) planned rate of return achieved;
  • (4) soundness of project formulation and execution; effect on gestation period and capital cost;
  • (5) adequacy of cost control; inefficiencies and wastage in raw materials;
  • (6) adequacy of purchase policies; piling up of inventory and redundancy in stores and spares;
  • (7) R&D and performance in adopting new processes and technologies;
  • (8) adequacy of repairs and maintenance;
  • (9) whether procedures are effective and economical;
  • (10) poor, insufficient or inefficient project planning.

Also asked (ICAI): MTP Nov 2022 S-I Q6(a) (Shravasti Ltd, ₹9,580 crore); MTP Dec 2021 S-II Q6(a) (Nalanda Ltd, ₹8,500 crore); SM TYK 3.
Q.trap: Also asked as SM TYK 3 (Sunlight Ltd, ₹5,750 crore) and RTP May 2026 Q16. Learn the ten issues as a list.

Q.q: The Government of India launched a rural development scheme for infrastructure, healthcare and education, providing funds to State Governments. The C&AG wants to ensure the funds were utilised for the identified purposes and that public interest has not been harmed. You are appointed by the C&AG to conduct the propriety audit of the funds used by the State Government for hospitals, school buildings and roads, and report on wastefulness in public administration and cases of improper, avoidable and infructuous expenditure. What functions as an auditor will be performed by you?
Q.a:
Functions of the auditor in propriety audit:

  • see that all expenditure incurred is properly planned;
  • see that the size and channels of expenditure are rightful and expected to give maximum results;
  • appraise whether the expenditure is likely to give optimum results;
  • see whether any substitute plan of action could bring about an improvement on current operations as well as return from capital expenditure;
  • examine the actions and decisions of management to see that they are conducive to public interest and meet the standards of conduct.
Q.trap: Giving the four principles of propriety instead. This question asks for the auditor's functions; Jan 2026 asked for the principles.

Q.q:
LNG Corporation, a government-owned entity operating liquefied natural gas, recently underwent a compliance audit by the C&AG, to assess whether its financial transactions, procurement activities and operations complied with relevant laws, regulations and internal guidelines.

(i) Explain the concept of compliance audit and its perspective. (2 marks)
(ii) What shall be the concern of the auditor when undertaking compliance audit? (2 marks)
Q.a:
(i) Compliance audit is the independent assessment of whether a given subject matter is in compliance with the applicable criteria, carried out by assessing whether activities, financial transactions and information comply in all material respects with the regulatory and other rules governing the entity.

Perspective: compliance auditing is part of a combined audit that may include other aspects. It is generally conducted (1) in relation with the audit of financial statements, (2) separately as individual compliance audits, or (3) in combination with performance auditing.

(ii) Concerns: (1) Regularity: adherence of the subject matter to formal criteria from relevant laws, regulations and agreements; (2) Propriety: observance of the general principles of sound financial management and the ethical conduct of public officials. Regularity is emphasised, but propriety is equally pertinent in the public sector.

Q.q: The Ministry of Information Technology has initiated a large-scale infrastructure project to improve rural connectivity under its "Digital Connect" programme. As part of the audit team you are to conduct a performance audit focused on assessing its efficiency. What key aspects should the auditor consider to determine whether resources are used efficiently?
Q.a:
Efficiency is the input-output ratio: in public spending it is achieved when output is maximised for minimum inputs, or input minimised for a given quantity and quality of output. The focus is on the processes that turn inputs into outputs.

Key aspects for "Digital Connect": (i) sound procurement practices are followed; (ii) resources are properly protected and maintained; (iii) human, financial and other resources are efficiently used; (iv) the optimum amount of resources (staff, equipment, facilities) is used to deliver the right quantity and quality in time; (v) programmes and activities are efficiently managed, regulated, organised and executed; (vi) efficient operating procedures are used; (vii) the programme's objectives are met cost-effectively.
Q.trap: Writing about all three Es. The question asks only for efficiency; give its definition and the seven aspects.

Q.q:
The Committee on Public Undertakings is examining the reports and accounts of a solar PSU and the C&AG's audit findings. Which of these are functions of COPU?

(i) examine accounts of autonomous and semi-autonomous bodies audited by the C&AG under the President's directions or a statute; (ii) examine the estimates to report possible economies, improvements in organisation, efficiency or administrative reform; (iii) examine the autonomy and efficiency of public undertakings and whether they follow sound business principles and prudent commercial practices; (iv) examine public enterprises through comprehensive appraisal of performance, including policies, programmes and financial working.
Q.why: (iii) and (iv) are COPU. (i) is a PAC function and (ii) is the Estimates Committee. (ICAI key: D; explanation from SM para 2.)
Q.a: Answer: (D) (iii) & (iv).

Q.q: XYZ & Associates LLP, appointed by the C&AG for a performance audit of Heavy Electricals Corporation, is asked to prepare an Audit Design Matrix for each audit objective. Which one of the following is not part of the Audit Design Matrix?
Q.why: The ADM columns are audit objective, audit questions, audit criteria, evidence, and data collection and analysis method. An audit programme is not one of them. (ICAI key: A.)
Q.a: Answer: (A) Audit programme.

Q.q: For a performance audit of Wind Power Ltd., the audit manager listed these planning steps: (1) understanding the entity/programme; (2) defining objectives and scope; (3) deciding audit approach; (4) developing audit questions; (5) determining audit criteria; (6) establishing timetable and resources; (7) preparing the Audit Design Matrix; (8) assessing audit team skills and outside expertise; (9) intimation of the audit programme. Select the correct sequence:
Q.why: SM order A–I: understand → objectives & scope → criteria → approach → questions → team skills → ADM → timetable → intimation, i.e. 1, 2, 5, 3, 4, 8, 7, 6, 9. (ICAI key: D.)
Q.a: Answer: (D) 1, 2, 5, 3, 4, 8, 7, 6, 9.

Q.q: In the performance audit of Wind Power Ltd., team members suggested methods: Mr P — descriptive analysis of an entity, scheme or programme; Mr Q — examination of available data on financials (earnings, revenue) or programme implementation (beneficiaries); Mr R — collecting information from members of a population to assess the interrelation of events and conditions; Mr S — review of systems for planning, conducting, checking and monitoring the activity. For whose method may the auditor be unable to work with complete data due to its high volume, so that sampling is required?
Q.why: Mr Q describes quantitative analysis, where the SM says sampling is needed when data volume is high. ICAI's key accepts (B) or (C): (C) is a survey, which also works on a sample of a population. P = case study, S = analysis of procedures.
Q.a: Answer: (B) Mr. Q (ICAI accepted B or C).

Q.q: Funds were approved to procure medical equipment for district hospitals. Audit reports show that 30% of the equipment remains unused due to lack of trained staff. Which committee can bring to the notice of the House that the particular policy is not leading to the desired results or is leading to waste?
Q.why: The Estimates Committee does not comment on a policy approved by Parliament, but where a policy is not leading to the desired results or leads to waste, it brings this to the notice of the House. (ICAI key: D.)
Q.a: Answer: (D) Estimates Committee.

Q.q: Classify each of the following as a form of public sector undertaking: (i) Indian Railways; (ii) Life Insurance Corporation; (iii) Kaveri Power Ltd., a company in which two State Governments together hold 55% of the paid-up capital; (iv) a wholly owned subsidiary of Kaveri Power Ltd.
Q.a:
Forms of PSUs: departmentally managed undertakings; government and deemed government companies under the Companies Act, 2013; corporations under specific Acts.

  • (i) Indian Railways: departmental undertaking, part and parcel of government activity.
  • (ii) LIC: statutory corporation set up under a specific Act.
  • (iii) Kaveri Power Ltd.: government company: not less than 51% held by one or more State Governments (s.2(45)).
  • (iv) Its subsidiary: also a government company, because the definition includes a subsidiary of a government company.
Q.trap: Thinking (iii) fails because no single government holds 51%. Holdings of several State Governments (and the Centre) are added together.

Q.q: A newspaper reports that the Union Cabinet plans to remove the C&AG by an executive order because it disagrees with his report on a PSU. It also proposes that the salary of the C&AG be fixed by the Finance Ministry. Comment.
Q.a:
Provision: Article 148: the C&AG is appointed by the President and can be removed only by a special procedure, on the ground of proven misbehaviour or incapacity; salary and conditions of service are determined by Parliament.

Analysis: Disagreement with an audit report is not proven misbehaviour or incapacity, and an executive order is not the special procedure. Fixing salary is Parliament's function, not the Finance Ministry's. These safeguards exist to protect the C&AG's independence.

Conclusion: Neither proposal is valid.
