Q.q: Mr. X is appointed Comptroller and Auditor General of India at the age of 62. Till when can he hold office? Can he leave earlier?
Q.a:
Provision: the C&AG's (Duties, Powers and Conditions of Service) Act, 1971: office for six years or up to the age of 65, whichever is earlier; he may resign at any time by a letter addressed to the President.

Conclusion: Mr. X holds office until he turns 65 (3 years, which is earlier than 6 years). He may resign earlier by writing to the President.

Q.q: A state-level autonomous research society receives about 80% of its funds as grants from the State Government. Its secretary claims the C&AG cannot audit it because it is not a department or a company. Comment.
Q.a:
Provision: Organisations under C&AG audit include Union and State departments, government companies and corporations, non-commercial autonomous bodies owned or controlled by the Union or States, and authorities and bodies substantially financed from Union or State revenues. The scope and extent of audit is determined by the C&AG.

Analysis: The society is substantially financed from State revenues.

Conclusion: It falls within the C&AG's audit; the secretary's claim is not correct.

Q.q: The Board of Directors of Bharat Tools Ltd., in which the Central Government holds 68%, appoints a CA firm of its choice as statutory auditor at the AGM and tells the firm to follow only the Standards on Auditing, ignoring any instructions from the C&AG. Comment.
Q.a:
Provision: For government companies (Government holding 51% or more), the auditors are firms of Chartered Accountants appointed by the C&AG, who gives directions on the manner of audit (s.143(5)), can comment on the audit report, and may conduct a supplementary audit or order a test audit.

Analysis: With 68% Government holding, Bharat Tools is a government company. The Board cannot appoint the auditor on its own, and the auditor cannot ignore C&AG directions; the report must include the directions, action taken and their impact.

Conclusion: Both the appointment and the instruction are contrary to the law governing government company audits.

Q.q: The statutory auditor of a State Government company received C&AG directions asking whether all accounting transactions are processed through the IT system. The auditor found some transactions processed outside the system but did not mention this in the report, saying it was an internal control matter. Comment.
Q.a:
Provision: Section 143(5): in a government company, the C&AG may direct the auditor on the manner of audit, and the auditor's report shall include the directions issued, the action taken thereon and its impact on the accounts and financial statements.

Analysis: Processing transactions outside the IT system is exactly what the direction asked about. The auditor must report it, its implications on the integrity of accounts and any financial impact.

Conclusion: The auditor has not complied with s.143(5).

Q.q: The management of a Central PSU complains that the Audit Board appraising its performance is "a separate authority outside the C&AG" and that it finalised adverse findings without hearing the Ministry. Comment on the nature and working of Audit Boards.
Q.a:
Provision: Audit Boards are constituted by the IAAD for comprehensive appraisals of PSUs. They associate experts; discuss findings with the management and the controlling ministries/departments before finalisation; the C&AG includes their results in his reports. They have no separate legal entity and work under the C&AG's supervision and control.

Conclusion: The Board is not a separate authority. Finalising findings without discussion with management and the Ministry would depart from its procedure; management may raise this with the C&AG.

Q.q: A Parliamentary committee is examining whether moneys shown in a Ministry's accounts as spent on a highway programme were disbursed legally for that purpose, whether the spending was authorised, and whether funds moved between heads followed the rules. Which committee is this, and what are its duties?
Q.a:
Committee: the Public Accounts Committee (PAC).

Duties: to satisfy itself (i) that moneys were disbursed legally on the service or purpose to which they were applied; (ii) that the expenditure was authorised; (iii) that re-appropriation was made in accordance with the provisions. It also examines the accounts of autonomous and semi-autonomous bodies audited by the C&AG under the President's directions or a statute.
Q.trap: COPU does this for public undertakings; for a Ministry's spending it is the PAC.

Q.q: A member of the Estimates Committee wants the Committee to reject a policy of subsidised fertiliser that Parliament has already approved, because he personally disagrees with it. Evidence also shows the scheme leads to large wastage. Advise.
Q.a:
Provision: The Estimates Committee reports possible economies and reforms, suggests alternative policies, checks the money is well laid out and suggests the form of estimates. It does not comment on a policy approved by Parliament; but where there is evidence that a policy is not giving the desired results or is leading to waste, it must bring it to the notice of the House.

Conclusion: The Committee cannot reject the policy for personal disagreement, but on the evidence of wastage it should report this to the House.

Q.q: A Ministry argues that since the Committee on Public Undertakings did not take up the C&AG's report on its PSU for detailed discussion, it need not respond to the observations. Comment on the role of the C&AG and the committees.
Q.a:
Provision: The C&AG is the 'friend, philosopher and guide' of the financial committees; his reports form the basis of their work. Ministries must inform committees of action taken on recommendations (Action Taken Reports). For audit reports not discussed in detail, written answers are obtained from the Ministry and sometimes included in reports to Parliament.

Conclusion: The Ministry must still respond; audit reports are not taken lightly even if not deliberated upon in full.

Q.q: A CA firm auditing a State PSU on C&AG's behalf tells management: "Our job is only to see whether the accounts are true and fair and the rules are followed; operational efficiency and whether decisions served public interest are none of audit's business." Comment.
Q.a:
Provision: Audit of public enterprises is not restricted to financial and compliance audit: it extends to performance (economy, efficiency, effectiveness), propriety of management decisions and comprehensive appraisal. Government audit covers fiscal accountability (funds, sanctions, compliance, propriety) and managerial accountability (efficiency, economy, effectiveness). Audit also aims to help Government and management improve.

Conclusion: The statement is incorrect for PSU audit.

Q.q: A PSU's General Manager awarded a large contract without the Board's approval required by the delegation of powers, arguing the contractor offered the lowest price. Examine from the audit perspective.
Q.a:
Provision: In examining management decisions, the auditor checks that they were taken by the competent authority, after examining all aspects (economic, technological, public interest) on all relevant information and alternatives, and consistent with the enterprise's objectives.

Analysis: A low price does not cure lack of authority: the decision was not taken by the competent authority.

Conclusion: Audit should report the decision as irregular, and examine whether alternatives and all aspects were considered.

Q.q: The C&AG audits the performance of a State Road Transport Corporation, and the report goes to the State Legislature. Identify the three parties and the subject matter, criteria and subject matter information in this audit.
Q.a:
Three parties: Auditor: the SAI India (C&AG and IAAD, through the Accountant General). Responsible party: the Corporation and those charged with its governance. Intended users: the State Legislature and others for whom the report is prepared.

Subject matter: the Corporation's operations being evaluated (e.g. fleet utilisation). Criteria: the benchmarks (norms, targets, guidelines). Subject matter information: the outcome of measuring the operations against those criteria.

Q.q: Classify as attestation or direct reporting engagements: (i) the C&AG's audit of a PSU's annual financial statements; (ii) a performance audit where the audit team itself measures hospital bed utilisation against norms; (iii) a compliance audit where the auditor evaluates procurement against the procurement manual.
Q.a:
Attestation: the responsible party measures the subject matter and presents the information; the auditor concludes on it. Direct reporting: the auditor measures or evaluates the subject matter against the criteria.

  • (i) Attestation: financial audits are always attestation engagements.
  • (ii) Direct reporting: the auditor measures.
  • (iii) Direct reporting: compliance audits are generally direct reporting engagements.

Q.q: To meet a deadline, an IAAD audit party skipped documenting its evidence and did not communicate findings to the entity before reporting. Which principles of PSU audits were ignored?
Q.a:
Provision: The principles of PSU audits are (I) general principles: ethics and independence; professional judgement, due care and scepticism; quality control; audit team management and skill; audit risk; materiality; documentation; communication; and (II) principles related to the audit process: planning, conducting, and reporting and follow-up.

Conclusion: The party ignored the general principles of documentation and communication (and due care/quality control). Time pressure does not override them.

Q.q: What is the objective of a financial audit conducted by the C&AG, and what opinion is expressed?
Q.a: Financial audit is conducted to express an audit opinion on the financial statements and to enhance the confidence of intended users in them. The C&AG gives an opinion on whether the financial statements are prepared, in all material respects, in accordance with the applicable financial reporting framework; under a fair presentation framework, whether they present fairly or give a true and fair view. It is always an attestation engagement.

Q.q: During audit of a Central PSU, the C&AG's team finds that works contracts above the prescribed limit were awarded on nomination instead of open tender, contrary to the PSU's own procurement rules and Government guidelines. Identify the audit and its concerns.
Q.a:
Type: Compliance audit: whether activities and transactions comply, in all material respects, with the rules governing the entity.

Concerns: Regularity: nomination instead of tender breaches the formal criteria in the procurement rules and guidelines. Propriety: whether the award observed sound financial management and ethical conduct of officials.

Conclusion: The non-compliance should be reported, with the entity's response.

Q.q: In a performance audit of a rural housing scheme, the team finds that beneficiary selection did not follow the scheme guidelines, and houses are incomplete. Explain how compliance auditing relates to the performance audit here.
Q.a:
Compliance auditing may be conducted with the financial audit, separately, or in combination with performance auditing. When part of a performance audit, compliance is seen as one aspect of economy, efficiency and effectiveness; non-compliance may be the cause of, an explanation for, or a consequence of the state of the activities audited.

Here, non-compliance with selection guidelines may explain poor outcomes (incomplete houses, wrong beneficiaries), so it is reported as part of the performance findings.

Q.q: A PSU hired consultants at rates 40% above the rates available from other empanelled consultants of equal quality, and bought spares in quantities far above requirement. Which aspect of performance audit is involved? What questions would the auditor ask?
Q.a:
Aspect: Economy: minimising the cost of resources used, having regard to appropriate quantity and quality, at the best price, acquired in due time.

Questions: Have the best prices been obtained for consultancy services? Were resources acquired in appropriate quantity and quality at the best price? Has there been waste of resources in achieving the output?

Q.q: A skill-training programme met its target of training 1 lakh youth, but only 8% got jobs, against an objective of 50% placement. Which aspect of performance audit is examined, and what may the auditor assess?
Q.a:
Aspect: Effectiveness: the extent to which objectives are achieved; intended vs actual impact.

Assess: whether objectives and means are proper; the extent of results achieved; whether observed impacts are due to the programme or other causes; factors inhibiting performance; overlap with other programmes; alternatives considered; adequacy of monitoring and reporting systems; ways to make it work better.

Conclusion: Output (training) was achieved but the outcome (placement) was not, which is an effectiveness failure.
Q.trap: Meeting the training target is output, not outcome. Effectiveness looks at objectives achieved.

Q.q: In a performance audit of a metro rail project, the Accountant General engaged a structural engineer and stated in the report that "the engineer is responsible for the technical conclusions". Comment.
Q.a:
Provision: While planning a performance audit (step F), the team decides where outside expertise is needed. Though the Accountant General may use the work of an expert, he retains full responsibility for the expression of opinion in the auditor's report.

Conclusion: The statement shifting responsibility to the engineer is not correct.

Q.q: Midway through a performance audit, the audit team changed its objectives and extended the audit to two more districts without recording reasons. The entity was also not informed of the audit schedule in advance. Comment.
Q.a:
Provision: (I) Intimation: audited entities must be told of the planned audit, its scope, team and tentative schedule well before commencement, and acknowledgement recorded. Objectives may be refined as the audit progresses, but reasons must be recorded and approved by the competent authority; the programme stays flexible.

Conclusion: Both the failure to intimate and the unrecorded change of objectives depart from the planning requirements.

Q.q: For a performance audit of a mid-day meal scheme, which audit approach methods would you use to (i) review how the scheme's monitoring system works, (ii) gauge beneficiaries' satisfaction, and (iii) test the scheme's database of 50 lakh beneficiaries?
Q.a:
(i) Analysis of procedures: review of the systems for planning, conducting, checking and monitoring the activity.

(ii) Surveys: collecting information from members of a population on predetermined parameters.

(iii) Use of existing data tested for correctness and completeness, with quantitative analysis using sampling because of the high volume.

Other methods: case studies, analysis of results (output-input).

Q.q: Distinguish comprehensive audit from performance audit as conducted by the C&AG in PSUs.
Q.a:
Performance audit examines the economy, efficiency and effectiveness of a government organisation, programme, activity or function.

Comprehensive audit is an efficiency-cum-performance appraisal of the undertaking as a whole, beyond what internal and statutory auditors cover. It combines financial, compliance and performance audit for a holistic assessment of whether objectives, value for money and targets were achieved (capital cost, capacity utilisation, rate of return, project execution, cost control, purchases, R&D, maintenance, procedures, planning). It is conducted by Audit Boards and reported to Parliament.

Q.q: The CMD of a PSU sanctioned a supply contract to a firm owned by his brother-in-law at market rates, following all tender formalities. The Board also approved a 'performance bonus' for senior managers in addition to their agreed remuneration, though the company made losses. Examine from the propriety angle.
Q.a:
Provision: Propriety principles: (i) expenditure no more than the occasion demands; (ii) a sanctioning authority must not pass an order that directly or indirectly accrues to its own advantage; (iii) funds not used for the benefit of a particular person or group; (iv) no avenue kept open to indirectly benefit management personnel beyond agreed remuneration.

Analysis: The contract indirectly benefits the CMD's relative (principles ii and iii) even though formalities were met. The bonus in a loss year benefits management beyond agreed remuneration (principle iv).

Conclusion: Both are fit to be reported in propriety audit, although compliant with rules.

Q.q: An auditor criticised a PSU for buying crude oil forward three years ago because prices later fell, and called officers' air travel wasteful without checking whether rail travel was feasible. Comment on the approach.
Q.a:
Provision: Propriety has an element of subjectivity. Commercial decisions taken in a dynamic environment must be evaluated with reference to the circumstances when they were taken, not on hindsight; the auditor must reconstruct those circumstances. Air travel is not wasteful unless it is shown that rail travel was feasible and would have brought the same results.

Conclusion: The auditor's approach is not objective; such judgement would dampen management initiative and make propriety audit counter-productive.

Q.q: Why is it difficult to apply propriety audit, and how has the C&AG addressed this? Can the same norms be applied to a private company?
Q.a:
Difficulty: 'Propriety' is a moral term; auditing needs verifiable propositions, but standards of public interest, customs and conduct are not firm, so propriety audit is inherently subjective.

C&AG's response: it has developed norms of propriety for public expenditure, which give a basis for verifying government spending.

Private sector: these norms do not automatically apply, as private entities have different objectives; but if each entity framed its own propriety norms, taking note of its social impact, subjectivity would reduce and propriety audit could be introduced more widely.

Q.q: How does the C&AG report on State government companies and corporations to the State Legislatures? What do such State reports contain?
Q.a:
For certain specified States, the C&AG submits a separate audit report (commercial) to the legislature; for other States/UTs with legislature, there is a commercial chapter in the main audit report.

State reports contain results of appraisal of performance of selected companies/corporations, important individual instances of financial irregularities, wasteful expenditure and system deficiencies noticed by statutory auditors, and a general review of the working results of government companies and corporations. Reports are submitted to the Governor under Article 151.

Q.q: Which Article of the Constitution provides that, on the advice of the C&AG, the President prescribes the form in which the accounts of the Union and the States are kept?
Q.why: Art. 150 is the form of accounts. Art. 148 is appointment and removal, Art. 149 duties and powers, Art. 151 submission of reports to the President/Governor.
Q.a: Answer: (c) Article 150.

Q.q: In a PSU audit, the responsible party measures the subject matter against the criteria and presents the information, on which the auditor gathers evidence and expresses a conclusion. This is:
opts: A direct reporting engagement, typical of performance audits
An attestation engagement, as in every financial audit
A direct reporting engagement, as in every financial audit
An attestation engagement, as in every performance audit
Q.why: When the responsible party measures and presents, it is an attestation engagement. Financial audits are always attestation engagements; performance and compliance audits are generally direct reporting.
Q.a: Answer: (b)

Q.q: Which statement about Audit Boards set up in commercial audit is incorrect?
opts: They conduct comprehensive appraisals of public sector enterprises
They associate experts in disciplines relevant to the appraisal
They are separate legal entities independent of the C&AG
They discuss findings with management and ministries before finalisation
Q.why: Audit Boards have no separate legal entity; they work under the supervision and control of the C&AG.
Q.a: Answer: (c)

Q.q: Which of the following is not one of the parts of the C&AG's report on PSUs presented to Parliament?
opts: General review of working results of government companies and corporations
Results of comprehensive appraisals by the Audit Board
Resume of company auditors' reports under C&AG directions
Minutes of the Board meetings of each government company
Q.why: The four parts are: general review of working results; Audit Board appraisals; resume of company auditors' reports and comments on accounts; significant results of audits not taken up by the Audit Board.
Q.a: Answer: (d)

Q.q: Which of the following is a principle related to the audit process (not a general principle) of PSU audits?
Q.why: Audit-process principles are planning, conducting, and reporting & follow-up. Materiality, documentation and quality control are among the eight general principles.
Q.a: Answer: (b)

Q.q: In Government audit, audit of efficiency, economy and effectiveness is part of:
Q.why: Fiscal accountability covers provision of funds, sanctions, compliance and propriety; managerial accountability covers efficiency, economy and effectiveness (efficiency-cum-performance audit).
Q.a: Answer: (b)

Q.q: The Comptroller and Auditor General holds office for:
opts: 5 years or up to age 62, whichever is earlier
6 years or up to age 65, whichever is earlier
6 years or up to age 65, whichever is later
At the pleasure of the President
Q.why: C&AG's (Duties, Powers and Conditions of Service) Act, 1971: six years or up to 65 years of age, whichever is earlier. Removal only by the special procedure under Art. 148.
Q.a: Answer: (b)

Q.q: A committee must satisfy itself that moneys were disbursed legally for the purpose applied, that expenditure was authorised, and that re-appropriation followed the provisions. This committee is:
Q.why: These three duties are the PAC's. COPU exercises the same kind of control over public undertakings.
Q.a: Answer: (a)

Q.q: For audit reports that the financial committees could not discuss in detail, what happens?
opts: They lapse at the end of the session
Written answers are obtained from the Ministry concerned and sometimes included in the committees' reports
They are returned to the C&AG for re-audit
They are referred to the Audit Board
Q.why: Written answers are obtained from the Department/Ministry and sometimes incorporated in reports presented to Parliament/Legislature, so audit reports are not taken lightly.
Q.a: Answer: (b)

Q.q: In a PSU audit, the outcome of evaluating or measuring the subject matter against the criteria is called:
Q.why: Subject matter = what is measured; criteria = the benchmarks; subject matter information = the outcome of measuring the subject matter against the criteria.
Q.a: Answer: (c)

Q.q: "Has there been a waste of resources in achieving an output?" In a performance audit, this question tests:
Q.why: Economy questions (ECA manual): best prices for consultancy, cost of sickness absences, lowest transport cost, waste of resources in achieving an output.
Q.a: Answer: (a)

Q.q: How does the cost per job created by a training programme compare with similar costs elsewhere? This question relates to:
Q.why: Efficiency is the input-output ratio; comparing cost per job created is an efficiency question in the SM.
Q.a: Answer: (b)

Q.q: Assessing whether observed social and economic impacts are due to the policy or to other causes is part of auditing:
Q.why: Effectiveness: the extent to which objectives are achieved and the relationship between intended and actual impact, incl. whether impacts are due to the policy.
Q.a: Answer: (c)

Q.q: Which is the starting point for planning an individual performance audit?
Q.why: Step (A), understanding the entity/programme, is the starting point (SM 6.2; RTP Nov 2026 Q18).
Q.a: Answer: (b)

Q.q: Which of the following is NOT listed in the SM as a source for understanding the entity in a performance audit?
opts: Reports of the Committee on Public Undertakings
The statutory auditor's engagement letter with the entity
Q.why: Sources: entity documents, legislative documents (incl. PAC/COPU/Estimates Committee reports), policy documents, academic research, past audits, media coverage, special focus groups.
Q.a: Answer: (d)

Q.q: Audit criteria in a performance audit are best described as:
opts: The audit programme approved by the Accountant General
Reasonable and attainable standards of performance against which economy, efficiency and effectiveness are assessed
The financial reporting framework applicable to the PSU
The list of audit questions in hierarchy
Q.why: SM definition of audit criteria.
Q.a: Answer: (b)

Q.q: Which of the following is a source of audit criteria listed in the SM?
Q.why: Criteria sources: procedure manuals; policies, standards, directives and guidelines; criteria of same/other entities; expert opinion; scientific knowledge; management literature. The others are sources for understanding the entity.
Q.a: Answer: (b)

Q.q: A school building completed by a PSU is put to use only five years after completion. In propriety audit this is an example of:
Q.why: SM example: a school used five years after completion = avoidable expenditure; a telephone-exchange building not used for that purpose = infructuous.
Q.a: Answer: (b)

Q.q: Which is NOT one of the four principles of financial propriety?
opts: Expenditure not prima facie more than the occasion demands
Sanctioning authority's order must not accrue to its own advantage
Funds must not be used for the benefit of a particular person or group
Every expenditure must be approved by the C&AG in advance
Q.why: The C&AG does not pre-approve expenditure. The fourth principle is: no avenue kept open to indirectly benefit management/employees beyond agreed remuneration.
Q.a: Answer: (d)

Q.q: Compliance auditing is concerned with:
Q.why: Compliance auditing: regularity (laws, regulations, agreements) and propriety (sound financial management, ethical conduct of officials).
Q.a: Answer: (b)

Q.q: Within how many days of receiving the audit report may the C&AG conduct a supplementary audit of a government company under s.143(6)(a)?
Q.why: s.143(6)(a): within 60 days from the date of receipt of the audit report (ICAI MTP May 2023 S-I).
Q.a: Answer: (c)

method: Step 1 — Name the audit or rule

Open with the type of audit (financial, compliance, performance, comprehensive, propriety) or the authority (C&AG, COPU, PAC, Art. 151, s.143(5)) the facts point to. Examiners give a mark just for identifying it correctly.
Give ICAI's definition in its own words, e.g. 'Compliance audit is the independent assessment of whether a given subject matter is in compliance with the applicable criteria.'
Link each fact to the definition, then give the list the question asks for (3Es, planning steps A–I, sources, issues (a)–(j), report parts). Use ICAI's headings; they are the marking points.
End with a clear line: 'Hence, it is a performance audit', 'the C&AG's rejection is in order', 'the report goes to the Governor'.
